subject: history
text: Who authored the novel Hard Times published in 1854 which deals with the grim reality of industrial towns of England in the mid-19th century?
explanation: Charles Dickens wrote 'Hard Times' (1854). The novel shows how life in the smoky, crowded factory towns of England (Coketown) was harsh for workers during the Industrial Revolution. Marx and Engels wrote about capitalism, but not this novel.

subject: history
text: Located in North Delhi Ridge and erected in 1863, the official memorial to commemorate the Revolt of 1857 in Delhi was called:
explanation: The memorial on the Delhi Ridge, built in 1863, remembers the British soldiers who died in the siege of Delhi in 1857. The British called the revolt the 'Mutiny', so the monument was named the Mutiny Memorial.

subject: history
text: Which of the following was a peasant revolt?
explanation: The Taiping Rebellion (1850-64) in China was a huge uprising of poor peasants against the Qing rulers and landlords, led by Hong Xiuquan. The Arab Revolt was against the Ottomans, the Boxer Rebellion was against foreigners, and the Cuban revolt was for freedom from Spain.

subject: history
text: What was the main cause of the economic crisis in France that led to the revolution?
explanation: The Third Estate (peasants and middle class) paid heavy taxes, while the clergy and nobles were exempt. Because taxes were so unequal and the state was already in debt, France ran out of money. This unfair tax system was the main cause of the financial crisis.

subject: history
text: Safety-valve theory of Indian National Congress’ formation was based on AO Hume’s biography where the author mentioned seven secret volumes about the seething discontent among the Indian masses. Who was this biographer of AO Hume?
explanation: William Wedderburn wrote the biography of A.O. Hume. The Safety Valve Theory says the Congress was set up in 1885 to give educated Indians a peaceful outlet for their anger, so that it would not burst out in violence like 1857.

subject: history
text: What was one of the first industries to be mechanised during the Industrial Revolution?
explanation: Textile (cotton) was the first industry to be mechanised. Inventions like the spinning jenny, water frame and power loom moved spinning and weaving from homes into factories, and the Industrial Revolution began here.

subject: history
text: Which of the following CANNOT be considered as one of the consequences of Industrial Revolution?
explanation: Factory workers had low wages, long hours, child labour and crowded slums, so 'prosperity among the working class' was NOT a result. Imperialism, mass production and the replacement of handicrafts by machines were all real consequences.

subject: history
text: Which of the following labour associations was founded by Anasuya Sarabhai?
explanation: Anasuya Sarabhai, a social worker from Ahmedabad, started the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (1920) after the mill workers' strike of 1918, which Gandhiji supported. The other names are different trade bodies.

subject: history
text: In which year did James Watt improve the steam engine?
explanation: James Watt improved the steam engine in 1769 by adding a separate condenser, which made it much more efficient. This engine powered factories and later trains and ships.

subject: history
text: Franklin D Roosevelt's National Recovery Administration was formed as part of which of the following Acts?
explanation: The National Recovery Administration (NRA) was created under the National Industrial Recovery Act, 1933, a part of Roosevelt's New Deal. It made industries follow fair codes for wages, hours and prices to fight the Great Depression.

subject: history
text: As part of the New Deal policy, President Franklin D Roosevelt helped pass many acts, and Wagner Act (1935) was one of them. It deals with which of the following?
explanation: The Wagner Act (National Labor Relations Act, 1935) gave workers the legal right to form labour unions and bargain with employers. It was part of the New Deal.

subject: history
text: The popular Urdu novel, 'Miratul-Uroos (The Bride's Mirror)' was written by:
explanation: 'Miratul-Uroos' (The Bride's Mirror, 1869) was written by Nazir Ahmad. It is an early Urdu novel that promoted education for girls and better manners for women in the home.

subject: history
text: The Revolt of 1857 began on 11 May 1857 in Delhi. When was Delhi recaptured by the British forces?
explanation: The revolt began in Meerut and Delhi on 10-11 May 1857. The British forces took Delhi back in September 1857 after a long siege, and the last Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar was captured.

subject: history
text: What type of monarchy was characteristic of the ancien regime of France on the eve of the French Revolution of 1789?
explanation: Before 1789 France was an absolute monarchy under the Bourbon king Louis XVI. The king held all the power and was not bound by any constitution or elected assembly.

subject: history
text: The theory of Safety Valve Theory is related to the:
explanation: The Safety Valve Theory explains why the Indian National Congress was formed (1885). It says the Congress gave educated Indians a safe outlet for their discontent so that the British rule would not face another violent revolt.

subject: history
text: The Dawes Plan of 1924 dealt with which of the following?
options: Scheme of repayment of reparation by Germany
explanation: The Dawes Plan (1924) reorganised how Germany would pay its World War I reparations. It reduced the yearly payments and gave Germany American loans to rebuild its economy.

subject: history
text: The first cotton mill in India was established in _______.
explanation: The first cotton mill in India was set up at Fort Gloster near Calcutta in 1818. Later Bombay became the main centre of the cotton textile industry, so many students get confused between the two.

subject: history
text: Champaran movement (1916) against indigo cultivation was to raise the issue against the system known as:
explanation: In Champaran (Bihar), peasants were forced by British planters to grow indigo on part of their land under the Tinkathia system (3 out of every 20 parts). Gandhiji led the Champaran movement against this system.

subject: history
text: From where was VD Savarkar's 'The Indian War of Independence' (1909) published?
explanation: V.D. Savarkar's 'The Indian War of Independence' (1909), about the revolt of 1857, was published from London, where Savarkar was studying and active in revolutionary work. The British banned it.

subject: history
text: The Factory Act of ________ in England limited the labour by young children to 8 hours per day.
explanation: The Factory Act of 1833 in England limited the working hours of children (9-13 years) and banned the employment of children under 9 in textile mills. It is an important early law to protect child workers.

subject: history
text: Which of the following is NOT true about Socialism?
options: Socialism was the direct result of Industrial Revolution.
Socialism was a direct challenge to Capitalism.
Socialism did not propagate the unity of working class.
explanation: Socialism was built on the unity of the working class, so the statement that it 'did not propagate the unity of working class' is wrong. Socialists wanted workers to unite to challenge capitalism.

subject: history
text: To oppose the White Army during the Russian Civil War, which of the following leaders established the Red Army in January 1918?
explanation: Leon Trotsky organised the Red Army in January 1918 as the Bolshevik fighting force. It fought the anti-Bolshevik White Army in the Russian Civil War.

subject: history
text: Who among the following were NOT entitled to separate electorates under the Communal Award of 1932?
explanation: The Communal Award (1932) gave separate electorates to Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans and the Depressed Classes. Buddhists were not included.

subject: history
text: After the French were defeated by the German army in the Second World War, a new puppet government supported by Germany was established in France. Who headed this government?
explanation: After France fell to Germany in 1940, a puppet government was set up in the town of Vichy and led by Marshal Philippe Petain. Charles de Gaulle, in contrast, led the Free French who kept fighting Germany.

subject: history
text: What does 'the Right to Self-determination', which became part of the international communist movement especially after the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917, literally mean?
options: Right of the colonies to liberate themselves from the colonial rule
Right of worker to form trade unions
Right of the European nations to form democratic governments
Right of individuals to propagate socialist ideas
explanation: After the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917, communists (Lenin) supported the right of colonies to be free from colonial rule. So 'self-determination' means the right of colonised people to liberate themselves.

subject: history
text: Due to the colour of their shirts, Italian fascists were also known as:
explanation: Mussolini's Italian fascists wore black shirts, so they were called Blackshirts. Do not confuse with the Brown Shirts (Hitler's Nazi SA) or the Red Shirts (Garibaldi's volunteers).

subject: history
text: Who among the following suppressed the rebellion in Banaras during the Revolt of 1857?
explanation: Colonel James Neill crushed the revolt at Banaras (and Allahabad) in June 1857 with great cruelty. Havelock and Campbell were involved in Kanpur and Lucknow, and Hugh Rose in central India and Jhansi.

subject: history
text: The term 'Blinkered Historiography', in terms of historiography of Indian nationalism, has been used by:
explanation: Ranajit Guha, founder of the Subaltern Studies group, criticised the elite-centred writing of Indian nationalism as 'blinkered historiography'. He argued that the role of common people was ignored.

subject: history
text: What was the immediate cause of the outbreak of World War I?
explanation: The immediate cause of World War I was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. The Moroccan crises and Balkan wars were earlier tensions (long-term causes).

subject: history
text: The Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) founded in Chicago in June 1905 was formed during:
explanation: The Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) was founded in Chicago in 1905, during the period of the Second International (1889-1916), the international body of socialist and labour parties.

subject: history
text: Among the different sections of society, which of following was exempted of Kings Law in France before 1789?
explanation: In France before 1789 the clergy (and nobles) were privileged and exempt from most taxes, while the Third Estate (peasants, workers, middle class) paid them. This inequality was a major cause of the Revolution.

subject: history
text: Which of the following Acts established a bicameral legislature at the Centre for the first time?
explanation: The Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) created a two-house (bicameral) central legislature for the first time: the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly. It also introduced dyarchy in the provinces.

subject: history
text: Which dynasty ruled France during the French Revolution?
explanation: The Bourbon dynasty ruled France during the Revolution of 1789, and Louis XVI was its king. Valois and Habsburg were other European royal families, and Bonaparte came later.

subject: history
text: Who was the representative of the Indian National Congress to the International Congress against Colonial Oppression and Imperialism held in Brussels in February, 1927?
explanation: Jawaharlal Nehru represented the Indian National Congress at the International Congress against Colonial Oppression and Imperialism at Brussels (1927). This meeting led to the League Against Imperialism.

subject: history
text: Who among the following is remembered for the emancipation of serfs in Russia?
explanation: Tsar Alexander II freed the serfs in Russia in 1861. The reform was meant to modernise the country, but many peasants remained poor, which kept unrest alive.

subject: history
text: Which of the following constitutions granted the emergency powers to the President of Germany to deal with economic depression?
explanation: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution allowed the German President to take emergency powers. It was used during the economic crisis, and Hitler later used it to end civil rights and take control.

subject: history
text: Who invented the incandescent electric light bulb?
explanation: Thomas Edison invented the practical incandescent electric light bulb (1879). Graham Bell is linked to the telephone, Marconi to wireless radio and Isaac Singer to the sewing machine.

subject: history
text: Which of the following statements about the Indian capitalist class during the struggle for independence is INCORRECT?
options: It accounted for over 80% of the deposits in the organised banking sector at the onset of independence.
It had captured most of the domestic market at the onset of independence.
It wholeheartedly supported the Indian National Congress in all its struggles.
It experienced rapid growth First World War onwards.
explanation: The Indian capitalist class did NOT support the Congress fully in every struggle. Many industrialists supported the freedom movement at times, but they also stayed cautious and sometimes opposed radical movements. The other statements about their economic growth are true.

subject: history
text: Who wrote Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind (1858)?
explanation: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan wrote 'Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind' (Causes of the Indian Revolt, 1858). He argued that British policies and lack of understanding caused the revolt, not just a Muslim conspiracy.

subject: history
text: The Hindu Widows Remarriage Act was passed in ______.
explanation: The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act was passed in 1856, after long efforts by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar. It made it legal for Hindu widows to remarry.

subject: history
text: All India Trade Union Congress was formed in ______.
explanation: The All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC), the first national trade union body of India, was formed in 1920 in Bombay. Lala Lajpat Rai was its first president.

subject: history
text: Who was the Commander-in-Chief of the British forces when the Revolt of 1857 broke out in May?
explanation: George Anson was the Commander-in-Chief of the British forces in India when the revolt began in May 1857. He died of cholera soon after, and Sir Patrick Grant and Colin Campbell later led the army.

subject: history
text: Which of the following is INCORRECTLY matched in relation with caste movements?
explanation: The Nadars were a caste movement in Tamil Nadu (Travancore), not Maharashtra. The other pairs are correct: Chamars in Punjab, Ezhavas in Kerala, Namasudras in Bengal.

subject: history
text: What was the main feature of the famous Bombay Plan?
options: Endorsement of comprehensive land reforms and cooperativisation
Promotion of a purely free-market economy
explanation: The Bombay Plan (1944) was made by Indian industrialists. It wanted the state to take an active role in developing basic industries and infrastructure, so 'state intervention' is its main feature. It was not a plan for a free market.

subject: history
text: Published in 1770, who wrote 'The History of Hindostan'?
explanation: Alexander Dow wrote 'The History of Hindostan' (1770), based on a translation of a Persian history. Do not confuse with James Mill's 'History of British India' (1817).

subject: history
text: The Great Fear in French Revolution was related to which of the following?
explanation: The Great Fear (July-August 1789) was a wave of panic in the French countryside. Peasants, afraid of nobles' hired armies, attacked castles and burned records of feudal dues. It is thus linked to peasant revolts.

subject: history
text: The first jute mill in India was started in _______.
explanation: India's first jute mill started at Rishra in Bengal in 1855. Bengal became the centre of the jute industry because jute was grown in the region and Calcutta was a major port.

subject: history
text: Who among the following did NOT belong to the Swaraj Party?
explanation: The Swaraj Party (1923) was formed by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru, and S.C. Mitra was a member. Subhas Chandra Bose was in the Congress and was not part of the Swaraj Party.

subject: history
text: The Paris Commune was held in the year ______.
explanation: The Paris Commune was a workers' government that ruled Paris for a short time in 1871 (March-May), after France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War. It was crushed by the French army.

subject: history
text: A long-standing demand of the nationalist leaders for a simultaneous recruitment exam for ICS in India was accepted and the first exam was held in 1922. In which city was the exam held?
explanation: After long demands by Indian nationalists, the first ICS exam in India was held in 1922, at Allahabad. Before this, the exam was held only in London, which made it very difficult for Indians to take part.

subject: history
text: What was the original name of the Russian leader Stalin?
explanation: Stalin's original name was Joseph Vissarionovich Dzhugashvili. 'Stalin' means 'man of steel' and was a name he took later. Vladimir Ulyanov was the original name of Lenin.

subject: history
text: The Italian Fascist Party in 1919 was founded by:
explanation: Benito Mussolini founded the Italian Fascist Party in 1919 and became Italy's dictator in 1922. Hitler led the Nazi Party in Germany, while Garibaldi and Mazzini were 19th-century leaders of Italian unification.

subject: history
text: Which of the following recognised the Muslim demand for a separate electorate?
explanation: The Lucknow Pact (1916) between the Congress and the Muslim League accepted the Muslim demand for separate electorates (already given by the Morley-Minto Reforms, 1909). It also showed Hindu-Muslim unity against British rule.

subject: history
text: Maulvi Ahmad Shah led the revolt in:
explanation: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah (Ahmad Shah) was the great leader of the revolt at Faizabad in Awadh. He was also called the 'Lighthouse of the Rebellion' and was respected by both Hindu and Muslim rebels.

subject: history
text: Which of the following was NOT written by Karl Marx?
explanation: Karl Marx wrote 'Das Kapital', 'The Civil War in France' and (with Engels) 'The Communist Manifesto'. 'Genesis of War' is not his work.

subject: history
text: When did Karl Marx deliver the inaugural address to the International Working Men's Association also known as the First International?
explanation: The International Working Men's Association (First International) was formed in London in 1864, and Marx wrote its inaugural address the same year. It was an early attempt to unite workers of many countries.

subject: history
text: Who was the President of the United States of America when the atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August 1945, respectively?
explanation: Harry S. Truman was the US President when atom bombs were dropped on Hiroshima (6 Aug 1945) and Nagasaki (9 Aug 1945). He became President in April 1945 after Roosevelt died.

subject: history
text: In which of the following cities was the Charter of the United Nations formulated?
explanation: The UN Charter was drawn up at the United Nations Conference in San Francisco (April-June 1945) and signed on 26 June 1945. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945.

subject: history
text: Which of the following did NOT get representation in the Russian local council, the Zemstvo?
explanation: The Zemstvo (local councils created in 1864 by Alexander II) had representatives of landlords, peasants and the middle class (townspeople). The clergy did not have a separate representation.

subject: history
text: To which infantry did sepoy Mangal Pandey belong?
explanation: Mangal Pandey was a sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry. He attacked British officers at Barrackpore in March 1857 and was hanged in April 1857, which is often called a spark before the revolt.

subject: history
text: When was the Crystal Palace Exposition (also known as the first World Fair), which was seen as a symbol of the new industrial age, held?
explanation: The Great Exhibition at the Crystal Palace, London, was held in 1851. It displayed the machines and goods of the Industrial Revolution and is seen as the first World Fair.

subject: history
text: Who among the following introduced the Doctrine of Lapse?
explanation: Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General 1848-56) introduced the Doctrine of Lapse. Under it, a princely state without a natural male heir could be annexed by the British, e.g. Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur.

subject: history
text: Which of the following statements about the Revolt of 1857 is NOT true?
options: The southern part of India remained unaffected during the revolt.
The armies of Punjab and Bombay remained loyal to the British.
The revolt was fierce in Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow and central India.
Bengali intellectuals actively supported the rebels.
explanation: Bengali intellectuals did not support the rebels. Many of them, being English-educated and benefiting from British rule, criticised the revolt. The other statements are true: the south was largely unaffected, and the armies of Punjab and Bombay stayed loyal.

subject: history
text: When did the National Constituent Assembly officially abolish feudal privileges in France?
explanation: On the night of 4 August 1789 the National Constituent Assembly abolished feudal privileges such as serfdom and the nobles' special rights. This was one of the first major steps of the Revolution.

subject: history
text: What was the main cause of the Great Depression?
explanation: The Great Depression is most closely linked to the Wall Street stock market crash (October 1929) in the USA. Share prices collapsed, banks failed and the crisis spread across the world.

subject: history
text: Who was responsible for the Partition of Bengal in 1905?
explanation: Lord Curzon (Viceroy) partitioned Bengal in October 1905. This led to the Swadeshi and Boycott movements. The partition was cancelled in 1911.

subject: history
text: Who among the following held the view that the Revolt of 1857 was a 'Muslim conspiracy'?
explanation: Sir James Outram, a British officer, called the revolt of 1857 a 'Muslim conspiracy' that used Hindu grievances. Other historians disagree, as Hindus and Muslims both took part.

subject: history
text: Who wrote the book 'History of British India'?
explanation: James Mill wrote 'A History of British India' (1817). He divided Indian history into Hindu, Muslim and British periods, which is a division still debated.

subject: history
text: In which part of Europe did the Industrial Revolution start first?
explanation: The Industrial Revolution first began in Western Europe, specifically in Britain, in the 18th century. It later spread to other parts of Europe and the world.

subject: history
text: In the first half of the 19th century, many industrial workers and artisans in England broke machines in protest. What term is used for those persons?
explanation: The Luddites were English workers who broke machines in the early 1800s because they feared the machines would take their jobs and lower their wages. Chartists demanded political rights and had a different aim.

subject: history
text: In the context of the traditional hierarchy of French society before the Revolution of 1789, what does the term 'first estate' mean?
explanation: In old French society the First Estate was the clergy, the Second Estate the nobility, and the Third Estate everyone else (peasants, workers and the middle class).

subject: history
text: Who was considered the imaginary leader of the violent movement that protested against the industrialisation and mechanisation of the textile industry in Great Britain?
explanation: The Luddites followed an imaginary leader called 'General Ludd' (or Ned Ludd) whose name was used to sign letters and threats. John Kay, on the other hand, invented the flying shuttle.

subject: history
text: Which Reform Act in England gave the right to vote to agricultural labourers?
explanation: The Reform Act of 1884 (Third Reform Act) in England gave the vote to agricultural labourers, extending the right to men in the countryside. The 1832 Act helped the middle class and the 1867 Act helped urban workers.

subject: history
text: The journal 'Asiatick Researches' was associated with which of the following?
explanation: 'Asiatick Researches' was the journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, founded by William Jones in 1784. It published studies on Indian history, languages and culture.

subject: history
text: Which of the following statements regarding the development of modern Indian industry in the first half of the twentieth century is NOT true?
options: It was supported by European bankers through long-term loans.
It faced hostility from the colonial administration.
It faced competition from foreign products.
It was dependent on imported equipment.
explanation: The statement that Indian industry was supported by European bankers through long-term loans is NOT true. Indian industry mostly depended on Indian capital and faced hostility from colonial rulers, foreign competition and dependence on imported machinery.

subject: history
text: When was the Indian Fiscal Commission established?
explanation: The Indian Fiscal Commission was set up in 1921, and it recommended discriminating protection for Indian industry. It led to the tariff policy of the 1920s.

subject: history
text: Which of the following British generals defeated the Rani of Jhansi?
explanation: General Hugh Rose defeated Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi in 1858. She died fighting at Gwalior in June 1858.

subject: history
text: When did Britain abandon the concept of free trade, which had been the centre of its British economic policy since the 1840s?
explanation: Britain gave up free trade in 1931-32 during the Great Depression, when it introduced protective tariffs (Import Duties Act, 1932). Free trade had been its main policy since the 1840s.

subject: history
text: Which of the following countries did NOT participate in the Dumbarton Oaks Conference in 1944, which suggested forming an international organisation that would eventually become the United Nations?
explanation: The Dumbarton Oaks Conference (1944) was held by the USA, the UK, the USSR (Russia) and China. France was not a participant, though it later became a permanent member of the UN Security Council.

subject: history
text: Which of the following was NOT a revolutionary party in Russia?
explanation: The Social Revolutionaries, Bolsheviks and Mensheviks were all revolutionary parties in Russia. Kulaks were not a party but rich peasants (farmers who owned land).

subject: history
text: According to Karl Marx’s 1859 book ‘A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy’, which of the following is NOT a productive force?
explanation: In Marx's view, productive forces are the things used in production: labour power, machinery and raw materials. Ideology is part of the 'superstructure' (ideas and beliefs), not a productive force.

subject: history
text: The theory of Economic Determinism was propounded by:
explanation: Karl Marx put forward the theory of Economic Determinism (also called the materialist conception of history), which says that the economic system decides a society's politics, laws and culture.

subject: history
text: Baba Ramchandra, who emerged as a legendary peasant leader in north India in the 1920s, was originally from which place?
explanation: Baba Ramchandra was a Maharashtra-born peasant leader who led the Kisan Sabha movement in Awadh (Uttar Pradesh) in the early 1920s. He had earlier worked as an indentured labourer in Fiji.

subject: history
text: Which English economist left the British delegation in protest of the harsh treatment accorded to Germany in the Versailles negotiations?
explanation: John Maynard Keynes left the British delegation at the Paris Peace Conference (Versailles Treaty, 1919) because he felt the harsh reparations on Germany would harm Europe. He wrote 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace'.

subject: history
text: Who among the following became the first Muslim President of the Indian National Congress in 1887?
explanation: Badruddin Tyabji was elected President of the Indian National Congress in 1887 (Madras session), the first Muslim to hold this post.

subject: history
text: The title of Hitler's autobiography, 'Mein Kampf' means:
explanation: 'Mein Kampf' is German for 'My Struggle'. Hitler wrote it while in prison (1924) and it sets out his racist and extreme nationalist ideas.

subject: history
text: Which of following was NOT a Utopian Socialist?
explanation: Saint-Simon, Charles Fourier and Robert Owen were Utopian socialists who imagined ideal communities. James Mill was a utilitarian thinker and the author of 'History of British India'.

subject: history
text: The Ilbert Bill Controversy was related to the:
options: nature of education in British India
protection of Properties of Christians converted from Hinduism
judicial discrimination on the basis of race
explanation: The Ilbert Bill (1883) proposed that Indian judges could try Europeans. British people protested strongly, so the Bill was diluted. It showed racial discrimination in the courts and helped awaken Indian nationalism.

subject: history
text: Mangal Pandey belonged to which regiment?
explanation: Mangal Pandey belonged to the 34th Bengal Native Infantry regiment, stationed at Barrackpore near Calcutta. His act in March 1857 is seen as a spark before the great revolt.

subject: history
text: Which technique, patented in 1769, produced in England yarn strong enough to be used as both warp and weft?
explanation: Richard Arkwright patented the water frame in 1769. It produced strong cotton yarn that could be used for both warp and weft, and the machines were run by water power.

subject: history
text: Which invention revolutionised the textile industry by enabling large-scale production of thread?
explanation: The spinning jenny (James Hargreaves, 1764) let one worker spin several threads at once, so thread production grew quickly. The power loom was for weaving and the cotton gin removed seeds from cotton.

subject: history
text: 'Black Thursday' is related to:
explanation: 'Black Thursday' (24 October 1929) was the day the New York stock market crashed, and it marked the beginning of the Great Depression.

subject: history
text: During the French Revolution, people of which group held special positions in the French Church?
explanation: The clergy formed the First Estate and held special privileges in the Church: they were exempt from taxes and collected the tithe from the peasants.

subject: history
text: Who passed the Emancipation Reform of 1861 for the abolition of serfdom in Russia?
explanation: Tsar Alexander II issued the Emancipation Reform of 1861, ending serfdom in Russia. Peter the Great, Alexander I and Nicholas I did not abolish serfdom.

subject: history
text: Which proclamation was enforced by Queen Victoria after the suppression of the Revolt of 1857?
explanation: After the revolt, the Government of India Act, 1858 ended the East India Company's rule and gave the power to the British Crown. Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 announced this and promised equal treatment and no more annexation.

subject: history
text: Prepared by the leading capitalists of India in 1944-45, before independence, 'A Brief Memorandum Outlining A Plan of Economic Development for India' is popularly known by which name?
explanation: The Bombay Plan (1944-45) was a 'Brief Memorandum Outlining a Plan of Economic Development for India' drawn up by industrialists like J.R.D. Tata and G.D. Birla. It wanted a large role for the state in basic industries.

subject: history
text: Which was the last nation in Europe to abolish serfdom in 1861?
explanation: Russia was one of the last countries in Europe to abolish serfdom (1861 under Alexander II), while most of Western Europe had done it earlier, for example in France in 1789.

subject: history
text: Who made the first crude photograph?
explanation: Nicephore Niepce, a French inventor, made the first photograph around 1826-27, using a camera obscura and a plate coated with bitumen. Louis Daguerre later improved the process.

subject: history
text: Who were the Kulaks in the Soviet Union?
explanation: Kulaks were relatively rich peasant farmers in the Soviet Union. Stalin's collectivisation policy in the late 1920s and 1930s attacked them, and many were killed or deported.

subject: history
text: In which year was the British Labour Party founded?
explanation: The British Labour Party was founded in 1900 (as the Labour Representation Committee) to send working-class representatives to Parliament. It took the name 'Labour Party' in 1906.

subject: history
text: Who was the leader of the Revolt of 1857 in Bihar?
explanation: Kunwar Singh, an old zamindar of Jagdishpur, led the revolt of 1857 in Bihar even at the age of about 80. Rani Lakshmibai led in Jhansi and Tantia Tope in central India.

subject: history
text: Where was India's first iron and steel company established?
explanation: India's first major iron and steel company, the Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO), was set up by Jamsetji Tata at Sakchi (Jamshedpur) in 1907.

subject: history
text: The theory of historical materialism was propounded by:
explanation: Karl Marx put forward the theory of historical materialism, which says that the way a society produces goods (its economic base) shapes its history, politics and ideas.

subject: history
text: Read the following statements regarding Hitler and Nazi Germany carefully and select the incorrect statement.
options: After gaining power, Hitler assumed the title of "Fuhrer".
He obtained an electoral majority in the elections of 1928.
Hitler wrote 'Mein Kampf' while he was in prison.
After gaining power, he imprisoned and killed his opponents, communists and Jews.
explanation: Hitler did not win an electoral majority in 1928. In fact the Nazi Party won very few seats then and only rose after the Great Depression, and even in 1932 it did not have a majority. The other statements are true.

subject: history
text: 'Indian War of Independence', written by V.D. Savarkar, was first published in the year ______.
explanation: V.D. Savarkar's book 'The Indian War of Independence' on the revolt of 1857 was first published in 1909 from London. The British government banned it.

subject: history
text: Which of the following was a colleague of Karl Marx?
explanation: Friedrich Engels was Karl Marx's lifelong friend and colleague. They wrote the Communist Manifesto together in 1848. Robert Owen was a Utopian socialist and Foucault was a French philosopher.

subject: history
text: Which of the following countries was NOT among the Allied Powers?
explanation: France, Italy (from 1915) and England were Allied Powers in World War I. Bulgaria joined the opposing side, the Central Powers (with Germany and Austria-Hungary).

subject: history
text: Which two European powers signed a 10-year non-aggression pact in August 1939, before the start of the Second World War?
explanation: The USSR and Germany signed the Molotov-Ribbentrop Non-Aggression Pact in August 1939, just before World War II began. It was a 10-year pact but was broken by Germany in 1941.

subject: history
text: Which of the following rebel leaders killed a British woman during the revolt of 1857?
explanation: Nana Saheb (the adopted son of the last Peshwa, Baji Rao II) is held responsible in traditional accounts for the killing of British women and children at Kanpur in 1857 (the Bibighar incident). Kunwar Singh, Birjis Qadr and Tantia Tope were other rebel leaders.

subject: history
text: In which book was the theory of Scientific Socialism propounded?
explanation: Scientific Socialism was put forward by Marx and Engels in the Communist Manifesto (1848). They called their theory 'scientific' to separate it from the imaginary ideas of the earlier Utopian socialists.

subject: history
text: In which of the following sessions was the resolution on Fundamental Rights of the Indian National Congress passed?
explanation: The Karachi Session of the Congress (1931, presided by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel) passed the resolution on Fundamental Rights and Economic Policy. Lahore 1929 declared Purna Swaraj.

subject: history
text: Who wrote the political pamphlet 'What is to be done? Burning Questions of our Movement'?
explanation: 'What Is To Be Done?' (1902) was written by Vladimir Lenin. It argued for a small, disciplined party of professional revolutionaries.

subject: history
text: Who delivered the presidential address to the Congress in 1887?
explanation: Badruddin Tyabji presided over the Congress session at Madras in 1887 and was the first Muslim Congress president. Dadabhai Naoroji presided over 1886 (Calcutta) and A.O. Hume was the general secretary.

subject: history
text: In which year was the first Trade Union Act passed in the United Kingdom, which gave legal recognition to trade unions?
explanation: The Trade Union Act of 1871 in the United Kingdom gave legal recognition to trade unions and protected their funds. It was an important step in the rights of workers.

subject: history
text: Which of the following is NOT a contributor to the historical processes of marginalisation and political subordination of peasants?
explanation: Peasants were pushed to the margins by cultural segregation, economic exploitation and social isolation. Geographical boundaries are not a cause of their subordination.

subject: history
text: Who was the chairman of the Indian States Committee, formed to clarify the relationship between the Indian princely states and the British Raj?
explanation: The Indian States Committee (1927), also called the Butler Committee, was headed by Sir Harcourt Butler. It studied the relationship between the princely states and the British Paramount power.

subject: history
text: Which one of the following was NOT a reason behind the growth of the Industrial Revolution?
explanation: The growth of the Industrial Revolution was helped by new consumer goods, changes in how people bought and used goods and better ways of taking decisions in business. Religious patterns were not one of the reasons.

subject: history
text: Who was the founder of the Grand National Consolidated Trades Union?
explanation: Robert Owen, a Welsh social reformer and Utopian socialist, founded the Grand National Consolidated Trades Union in 1834, which tried to unite many workers into one large union.

subject: history
text: Who among the following was crowned as the King of Awadh by the rebel sepoys during the Revolt of 1857?
explanation: Birjis Qadr, the young son of the deposed Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, was proclaimed the ruler (Nawab) of Awadh by the rebels in Lucknow in 1857. His mother, Begum Hazrat Mahal, ruled on his behalf.

subject: history
text: Who among the following has NOT contributed to the development of wireless communication?
explanation: James Clerk Maxwell (theory of electromagnetic waves), Heinrich Hertz (proved radio waves) and Marconi (wireless telegraphy) all contributed to wireless communication. Winston Churchill was a British politician.

subject: history
text: Which American statesman said, 'Plant more wheat, wheat will win the war'?
explanation: 'Plant more wheat, wheat will win the war' was a slogan of US President Woodrow Wilson during World War I. It urged farmers to grow more food for the war effort.

subject: history
text: Who among the following wrote the book 'Bonded Histories' on the emergence of landless agricultural labourers during the colonial period?
explanation: 'Bonded Histories' (1990) is by Gyan Prakash. It studies how bonded labour (kamiauti) in colonial Bihar came about and affected agricultural labourers.

subject: history
text: Which of the following industrialists was a close associate of Mahatma Gandhi?
explanation: Jamnalal Bajaj, a well-known industrialist from Wardha, was a close associate of Gandhiji, and Gandhiji even called him his 'adopted son'. The others (like John Mathai) were linked to the Bombay Plan.

subject: history
text: During the Revolt of 1857, sepoy Mangal Pandey served in which of the following regiments?
explanation: Mangal Pandey was a sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry at Barrackpore. In March 1857 he attacked his British officers, and he was hanged in April 1857.

subject: history
text: In the context of the traditional hierarchy in French society before the Revolution of 1789, what does 'first estate' mean?
explanation: In pre-revolutionary France the First Estate was the clergy, the Second was the nobility, and the Third Estate was the rest of the people. Clergy had special privileges like tax exemption.

subject: history
text: Which of the following countries became the first industrial nation?
explanation: Britain was the first country to become an industrial nation, from the middle of the 18th century, because it had coal and iron, capital, colonies and skilled labour.

subject: history
text: In 1905, at the time of the Partition of Bengal, which of the following present-day Indian states was NOT a part of the Bengal Presidency?
explanation: In 1905, the Bengal Presidency included present-day West Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and Bangladesh. Chhattisgarh was then part of the Central Provinces and not of Bengal.

subject: history
text: Which sepoy regiment at Barrackpore refused the proposal to go to Burma by the sea route?
explanation: The 47th Native Infantry at Barrackpore refused to go to Burma by sea in 1824 because crossing the sea would make them lose caste. It was crushed harshly and is seen as an early sign of sepoy discontent.

subject: history
text: Who launched the New Deal recovery programmes to deal with the economic challenges of the Great Depression?
explanation: US President Franklin D. Roosevelt launched the New Deal (1933) to end the Great Depression. It brought bank reform, relief and public works. Hoover was the President before him, and Keynes was an economist.

subject: history
text: Which of the following is NOT included in the theory of alienation given by Karl Marx?
options: Man is alienated from other men.
Man is alienated from his own product.
explanation: Marx's theory of alienation says that under capitalism workers become alienated from their product, from other men and from themselves. Being alienated from 'materiality' is not part of it.

subject: history
text: When did the British Parliament pass the Government of India Act, 1858, which transferred the power to rule India from the East India Company to the British Crown?
explanation: The Government of India Act, 1858 was passed by the British Parliament on 2 August 1858. It ended the Company's rule and put India under the British Crown.

subject: history
text: Which countries were part of the Allied alliance during the First World War?
explanation: In World War I the Allied Powers included France, Britain and Russia. Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria formed the opposing Central Powers.

subject: history
text: When did Vladimir Lenin, the founder of the Bolsheviks, return to Russia after his exile?
explanation: Lenin returned to Russia from exile in April 1917 (after the February Revolution). He then presented his 'April Theses', calling for all power to the Soviets.

subject: history
text: The General Confederation of Labour (CGT), which was formed in 1895 to unite the trade union movement, belonged to which nation?
explanation: The General Confederation of Labour (Confederation Generale du Travail, CGT) was founded in France in 1895 to unite workers' unions.

subject: history
text: Which weapon significantly changed the nature of warfare during the First World War?
explanation: Tanks, first used in 1916, broke the deadlock of trench warfare and are the weapon that most changed the way World War I was fought. Poison gas, submarines and aircraft were also used but tanks are usually stressed.

subject: history
text: Who presided over the Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress in 1929?
explanation: Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the Lahore session of the Congress (December 1929), where the demand for Purna Swaraj (complete independence) was declared.

subject: history
text: In which year did Mussolini and Hitler sign the Rome-Berlin Axis?
explanation: Mussolini and Hitler formed the Rome-Berlin Axis in 1936 (it later became the Pact of Steel in 1939). This was an alliance of the two fascist dictators.

subject: history
text: Which type of politics did the Moderates adopt, which was criticised by the radical Congress leaders?
explanation: Radical (Extremist) leaders like Tilak, Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal criticised the Moderates' 'politics of prayers and petitions', meaning that they only made requests and did not take bold action.

subject: history
text: Which political party was mainly associated with the rise of socialism in Germany during the latter half of the 19th century?
explanation: In Germany the Social Democratic Party (SPD) was the main party that spread socialism in the second half of the 19th century. It was one of the strongest socialist parties in Europe.

subject: history
text: Who was the main leader of the Revolt of 1857 in Lucknow?
explanation: Begum Hazrat Mahal, the wife of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, led the revolt in Lucknow, and her son Birjis Qadr was declared Nawab.

subject: history
text: In the 20th century, near which place in Bengal in particular did 'muslin - a type of cotton cloth' originate?
explanation: Dhaka, in Bengal (now in Bangladesh), was famous for its fine muslin cotton cloth. Its delicate weaving was admired around the world.

subject: history
text: In which year was the All India Scheduled Castes Federation established?
explanation: Dr B.R. Ambedkar founded the All India Scheduled Castes Federation in 1942 to fight for the political rights of Dalits.

subject: history
text: Under which Act did the British give Muslims the privilege of a Separate Electorate in India?
explanation: The Morley-Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act, 1909) introduced separate electorates for Muslims. It is called the 'communal electorate' beginning, and Lord Minto is known as the 'father of communal electorate'.

subject: history
text: Who was the first woman President of the Indian National Congress?
explanation: Annie Besant became the first woman President of the Indian National Congress in 1917 (Calcutta session). Sarojini Naidu was the first Indian woman President in 1925.

subject: history
text: Which of the following businessmen was NOT a signatory of the famous Bombay Plan?
explanation: The Bombay Plan signatories included J.R.D. Tata, G.D. Birla, A.D. Shroff, Purshotamdas Thakurdas and others. Anand Mahindra, a modern businessman, obviously was not one of them.

subject: history
text: Who was the founder of the All India Dalit Class?
explanation: Dr B.R. Ambedkar is regarded as the founder of the Dalit organisations such as the Depressed Classes Federation, which fought for the political and social rights of Dalits.

subject: history
text: When was the Tennessee Valley Authority created to promote the economic development of the Tennessee Valley region?
explanation: The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) was created in 1933 as a part of Roosevelt's New Deal to build dams, generate electricity and develop the Tennessee Valley region.

subject: history
text: What was the law of 4 February 1794?
options: It was a law relating to the protection of private property in France.
It was a law that introduced a uniform system of weights and measures in France.
It was a decree that abolished slavery in the French colonial empire.
It was the 'French Civil Code' after the Revolution.
explanation: On 4 February 1794, the French National Convention abolished slavery in the French colonies. Napoleon later brought it back in 1802.

subject: history
text: Which of the following Presidents of the United States initiated the New Deal measures to overcome the problems caused by the Great Depression?
explanation: Franklin D. Roosevelt started the New Deal in 1933 to rescue the USA from the Great Depression, with measures such as relief, recovery and reforms. Hoover was the previous President.

subject: history
text: Which of the following states was NOT annexed under the 'Doctrine of Lapse'?
explanation: Rohilkhand was not annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse (it was taken over in 1801). Udaipur (in Chhattisgarh, 1852), Satara (1848) and Jhansi (1853) were annexed by Lord Dalhousie under the Doctrine of Lapse.

subject: history
text: Which of the following leaders did NOT belong to the Unionist Party of Punjab?
explanation: The Unionist Party of Punjab had leaders like Fazl-i-Husain, Sikandar Hayat Khan and Chhotu Ram. A.K. Fazlul Huq was a Bengal leader (Krishak Praja Party), not a Unionist.

subject: history
text: What was the peak period of the Great Depression?
explanation: The Great Depression was at its worst in 1929-1933. In these years prices, trade, jobs and incomes fell sharply, especially in the USA and Europe.

subject: history
text: When did the Bardoli Satyagraha take place?
explanation: The Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928 was led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel in Gujarat against an increase in land revenue. It succeeded and gave Patel the title 'Sardar'.

subject: history
text: In which year did the Great Depression begin?
explanation: The Great Depression began in 1929 with the Wall Street stock market crash in the USA. It lasted for about a decade.

subject: history
text: Which of the following Estates adopted the title of National Assembly during the French Revolution?
explanation: In June 1789 the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly. It said it represented the people of France, not the clergy or nobles.

subject: history
text: After which of the following movements was Vallabhbhai Patel given the title 'Sardar'?
explanation: Vallabhbhai Patel was given the title 'Sardar' by the women of Bardoli after the successful Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) against increased land revenue in Gujarat.

subject: history
text: Hitler propounded the concept that the German people lacked space for the 'healthy' expansion of the German people. Which German word did he use for this concept?
explanation: Hitler used the German word 'Lebensraum' (living space). He claimed Germany needed more land to expand, and this idea was used to justify attacks on Eastern Europe.

subject: history
text: Which of the following is NOT a law or act passed in England?
explanation: The Sickness Insurance Law of 1883 was passed in Germany under Bismarck, not in England. The Factory Act, the Trade Union Act and the Artisans Dwelling Act were English laws of the 1870s.

subject: history
text: When did socialists and trade unionists in Britain start the Labour Party?
explanation: The Labour Party in Britain was started by socialists and trade unionists in 1900 (as the Labour Representation Committee), to get working-class representatives into Parliament.

subject: history
text: Which city was first targeted with an atomic bomb in 1945?
explanation: The first atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945. Nagasaki was hit three days later, on 9 August 1945.

subject: history
text: After capturing Delhi in 1857, which British officer shot dead the sons of the Mughal emperor Bahadur Zafar?
explanation: After Delhi was recaptured in 1857, Captain William Hodson shot the sons and grandson of the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar at Humayun's Tomb, and Bahadur Shah was sent to Rangoon.

subject: history
text: On the founding day of the United Nations, how many countries had signed the Charter of the United Nations?
explanation: Fifty original members had signed the UN Charter in June 1945 and Poland signed later, making 51 original members. On 24 October 1945, when the UN came into existence, the 51 countries had signed the Charter.

subject: history
text: What was the Stakhanovite movement?
options: An armed militia movement against the atrocities committed by Soviet leader Joseph Stalin
A mass movement among workers in the Soviet Union that encouraged achieving record production output
A political reform movement within the Communist Party of the Soviet Union for restructuring and transparency
A cultural movement advocating fair treatment of minorities affected by the Russian Civil War
explanation: The Stakhanovite movement (1935) in the Soviet Union urged workers to break production records, named after the coal miner Alexei Stakhanov. The state used it to push industrial output.

subject: history
text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the Quit India Movement (1942)?
options: It demanded complete independence from British rule and called for widespread civil disobedience.
It was launched immediately after the First World War.
Its objective was to support the British war effort in India.
It resulted in the immediate end of British rule in India.
explanation: The Quit India Movement (August 1942, launched by Gandhiji with the slogan 'Do or Die') demanded an immediate end to British rule and involved mass civil disobedience. It did not end British rule immediately (India became free in 1947).

subject: history
text: Which of the following Governor Generals abolished the practice of Sati?
explanation: Lord William Bentinck, the Governor-General, abolished the practice of Sati in 1829, with the support of Raja Ram Mohan Roy.

subject: history
text: Where was the Indian Jute Mills Association established?
explanation: The Indian Jute Mills Association (IJMA) was set up at Calcutta in 1884 because the jute industry was located in and around Calcutta (Bengal).

subject: history
text: After winning the general election of 1971, the Congress government led by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi passed several acts/laws for industries and the economy. Which of the following is one of them?
options: Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act
explanation: The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA) was passed in 1973 after Indira Gandhi's win in 1971. Bank nationalisation (1969) and the MRTP Act (1969) came before the 1971 election, and the railways were nationalised earlier.

subject: history
text: Who described the state of Awadh as 'A cherry that will drop into our mouth one day'?
explanation: Lord Dalhousie called Awadh 'a cherry that will drop into our mouth one day'. It was annexed in 1856 by Dalhousie on the charge of misrule by Wajid Ali Shah, which angered the sepoys.

subject: history
text: Who among the following is known as the 'Father of the American Industrial Revolution'?
explanation: Samuel Slater, an English-born mill worker who carried British textile technology to the USA in 1789, is called the 'Father of the American Industrial Revolution'.

subject: history
text: Which of the following famous industrialists is called the 'Father of Indian Industry'?
explanation: Jamsetji Tata is called the 'Father of Indian Industry' as he set up India's first big steel plant, a hydroelectric project and the Taj Mahal Hotel and encouraged scientific education.

subject: history
text: Who led the revolt in Kanpur in 1857 and drove the British soldiers out of the city?
explanation: Nana Sahib led the revolt at Kanpur in 1857 and, with Tantia Tope's help, drove out the British for a while. Hazrat Mahal led Lucknow and Bakht Khan led Delhi's forces.

subject: history
text: Which of the following arguments was NOT made by Lala Lajpat Rai in his article in Young India regarding the establishment of the Congress?
options: The Congress was 'the brainchild of Lord Dufferin.'
He used the 'safety-valve theory' to attack the Moderates in the Congress.
The interests of India were primary and the interests of the British Empire were secondary.
The Congress was established mainly with the objective of saving the British Empire from danger.
explanation: In his Young India articles Lala Lajpat Rai called the Congress the 'brainchild of Lord Dufferin' and attacked the Moderates using the safety valve theory. He did not claim India's interests were primary, so option C is not his argument.

subject: history
text: In the Telugu-speaking regions of the Madras Presidency, a reform movement was started in support of widow remarriage, and the 'Society for Social Reform' was started in 1878. Who was behind this initiative?
explanation: Kandukuri Veeresalingam Pantulu started the widow remarriage movement in the Telugu region and set up the 'Society for Social Reform' in 1878. He also wrote the first Telugu novel.

subject: history
text: What does ASSOCHAM, India's oldest business apex chamber, stand for?
options: Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry in India
explanation: ASSOCHAM stands for the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India. It was founded in 1920 and is one of the oldest business bodies in India.

subject: history
text: Who wrote the book 'The Rights of Women' published in 1791, which elaborated the notion of equal rights for women?
explanation: Olympe de Gouges wrote the 'Declaration of the Rights of Woman and Citizen' (1791), demanding equal rights for women during the French Revolution. Mary Wollstonecraft's 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' came in 1792.

subject: history
text: When was the Permanent Settlement introduced?
explanation: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal. It fixed the land revenue permanently and made zamindars the owners of the land.

subject: history
text: What was the main goal of the National Industrial Recovery Act, 1933 in the United States?
options: To provide social security schemes for elderly citizens
To increase the industrial production of heavy goods
To generate employment for economic recovery and regulate industry
To provide financial assistance to farmers
explanation: The National Industrial Recovery Act (1933), part of the New Deal, aimed at recovery by creating jobs, fixing fair wages and prices and regulating industry.

subject: history
text: When was the Arms Act passed, under which Indians were prohibited from keeping arms?
explanation: The Arms Act of 1878, passed under Lord Lytton, forbade Indians from keeping arms without a licence, while Europeans and Anglo-Indians were exempt. It was a clear racial discrimination.

subject: history
text: Which important administrative change did the British implement in India after the suppression of the Revolt of 1857?
explanation: After 1857, the East India Company's rule ended and the British Crown took direct control of India, which is called the British Raj.

subject: history
text: On which date did the fall of the Bastille take place?
explanation: The Bastille prison in Paris was stormed by the people on 14 July 1789, which is regarded as the beginning of the French Revolution (celebrated as Bastille Day).

subject: history
text: Who is the author of the influential book 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money'?
explanation: 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' (1936) was written by John Maynard Keynes. He argued that governments should spend to fight unemployment during a depression.

subject: history
text: Who established the Bharat Stri Mahamandal in 1910 to promote women's education?
explanation: Sarla Devi Chaudhurani established the Bharat Stri Mahamandal at Allahabad in 1910 to spread women's education and improve their condition.

subject: history
text: In the context of socialism, what is the full form of 'LSI'?
explanation: LSI stands for Labour and Socialist International (1923), a group of social democratic parties formed after the First World War. It was a rival of the Communist International.

subject: history
text: Which one of the following is NOT a part of Karl Marx's philosophy regarding the schema of historical stages of society?
explanation: Marx described the stages of society as primitive communism, slavery, feudalism, capitalism and finally socialism/communism. Imperialism is not one of his stages.

subject: history
text: Which conference in 1945 resulted in the division of Germany into four occupied zones?
explanation: At the Potsdam Conference (July-August 1945) the Allies (USA, UK, USSR) decided the division of Germany into four occupation zones (also including France). Yalta earlier laid the plan.

subject: history
text: What did Karl Marx predict would ultimately happen to capitalist societies?
options: They would flourish and continue to expand indefinitely.
They would transform into feudal societies.
A proletarian revolution would overthrow them.
explanation: Marx predicted that capitalism would create class conflicts, and the working class (proletariat) would rise in a revolution and overthrow it.

subject: history
text: When did India become a member of the United Nations?
explanation: India was one of the original members of the United Nations, which it joined on 30 October 1945, even though it was still under British rule then.

subject: history
text: Which electoral law passed by the Italian Parliament changed the rules of general elections, giving Mussolini's Fascist Party a majority of legislators in the 1924 elections?
explanation: The Acerbo Law (1923) said the party with the most votes (at least 25%) would get two-thirds of the seats. It helped Mussolini's Fascists win a majority in the 1924 election.

subject: history
text: Which of the following thinkers did NOT influence the political ideas of Mahatma Gandhi?
explanation: Gandhiji was influenced by John Ruskin ('Unto This Last'), Leo Tolstoy and Ralph Waldo Emerson/H.D. Thoreau. Leonardo da Vinci was a Renaissance artist and did not influence his ideas.

subject: history
text: Which one of the following is NOT a demand/cause of the Russian Revolution?
options: Modernisation of Islam to lead their societies
Increase in wages and improvement in working conditions
Reduction of the working day to six hours
explanation: The demands during the Russian Revolution were for a constitution, higher wages, better working conditions and shorter working days. Modernising Islam was not one of them.

subject: history
text: Where did the British finally defeat Lakshmibai, the Rani of Jhansi?
explanation: Rani Lakshmibai was finally defeated by the British (General Hugh Rose) at Kota ki Serai near Gwalior in June 1858 and she died there fighting.

subject: history
text: Which of the following princely states was NOT annexed under the ‘Doctrine of Lapse’?
explanation: Hyderabad was not annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse (it remained a princely state until 1948). Jhansi, Nagpur and Satara were taken over by Lord Dalhousie under this doctrine.

subject: history
text: Which monarch was guillotined during the French Revolution?
explanation: Louis XVI was guillotined in January 1793. Louis XIV had died in 1715, and Napoleon was not a monarch executed in the Revolution.

subject: history
text: Which of the following is NOT a reason that led to the beginning of the Industrial Revolution in England?
explanation: The Industrial Revolution in England was helped by scientific and technological developments, closeness to the sea (trade) and rich coal and iron resources. Socialism was a reaction to industrialisation, not a cause.

subject: history
text: Who, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, was a trailblazer in Bengali theatre and collaborated closely with dramatist Girish Chandra Ghosh?
explanation: Binodini Dasi was a pioneering actress of Bengali theatre in the late 19th century and worked closely with Girish Chandra Ghosh. She was one of the first women stage stars in India.

subject: history
text: Who among the following was the first Indian to go to jail in performance of his duty as a journalist during the British rule?
explanation: Surendranath Banerjea, editor of 'The Bengalee', was jailed in 1883 for contempt of court, and was the first Indian journalist to go to jail for his writing.

subject: history
text: Which of the following is NOT true about the growth of modern Indian industry during the first-half of the twentieth century?
options: It faced hostility from Colonial administration
It was supported through Long Term Credits by European Bankers
It was dependent on imported equipments
explanation: The statement about long-term credit from European bankers is NOT true. Indian industry was mostly financed by Indian capital and often faced hostility, foreign competition and dependence on imported equipment.

subject: history
text: Who was the President of the United States during the Great Depression from 1929 to 1933?
explanation: Herbert Hoover was US President at the time of the Great Depression (1929-33), and Franklin D. Roosevelt took over in 1933 and started the New Deal.

subject: history
text: Which of the following were recommended by the Wood’s Despatch of 1854?
explanation: The Wood's Despatch (1854) recommended that elementary (primary) education should be in the vernacular languages, while English should be used for higher education. It also proposed universities in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.

subject: history
text: What type of socialism did the Fabian Society advocate?
explanation: The Fabian Society (founded in London in 1884) wanted socialism to come slowly through reforms and elections, not through revolution, which is called non-revolutionary or gradual socialism.

subject: history
text: What is the title of the book written by Adolf Hitler?
explanation: Adolf Hitler wrote 'Mein Kampf' ('My Struggle') in 1924-25. 'The Prince' is by Machiavelli, 'The Social Contract' by Rousseau and 'The Communist Manifesto' by Marx and Engels.

subject: history
text: Which of the following was NOT a reason behind the Revolt of 1857?
explanation: The revolt had causes like the land revenue system, Doctrine of Lapse and the zamindari system. The abolition of Sati (1829) was a social reform and was not a cause of the revolt.

subject: history
text: Who among the following was the British Prime Minister during the revolt of 1857?
explanation: Henry John Temple (Lord Palmerston) was the British Prime Minister during 1855-58, which covers the revolt of 1857.

subject: history
text: Who signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on behalf of the Bolshevik government?
explanation: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918) ended Russia's part in World War I. It was signed for the Bolshevik government by Grigori Sokolnikov, after Trotsky had left the negotiations.

subject: history
text: When did the event known as the Paris Commune occur?
explanation: The Paris Commune was the revolutionary workers' government of Paris in 1871 (March to May).

subject: history
text: Which of the following was NOT the main organ of the United Nations Organization?
explanation: The main organs of the UN are the General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, Trusteeship Council, International Court of Justice and Secretariat. The League of Nations was an earlier body which the UN replaced.

subject: history
text: The Drain of Wealth was described as 'the evil of all evils' by whom?
explanation: Dadabhai Naoroji, who wrote 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India', described the drain of wealth as 'the evil of all evils'. He explained how India's wealth flowed to Britain.

subject: history
text: Which of the following is NOT among the primary reasons for the rapid industrialisation of Britain?
options: Availability of many poor people from the villages to work in towns
People receiving their income in the form of goods
Expansion of a good transport network
Banks loaning money to set up large industries
explanation: Britain industrialised quickly because of a large pool of poor workers, good transport and bank loans. Being paid in the form of goods was not a reason, since industrial workers were paid in money.

subject: history
text: Who was the founder of Young Bengal group?
explanation: Henry Vivian Derozio, a teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta, founded the Young Bengal group in the 1820s-30s. His students questioned old customs and blind faith.

subject: history
text: What was Hilton-Young Commission?
options: A commission to inquire into the issue of separate electorates.
A commission to inquire into Indian currency and Rupee-Sterling exchange rate.
A commission to inquire into the issues of higher education in India.
A commission to inquire into affairs of the princely states.
explanation: The Hilton-Young Commission (1925-26) looked into India's currency and the rupee-sterling exchange rate. It recommended a gold bullion standard and led to the creation of the Reserve Bank of India.

subject: history
text: When did France and Great Britain sign the Anglo-French Commercial Treaty that became one of the reasons for the French Revolution.
explanation: The Anglo-French Commercial Treaty (Eden Treaty) was signed in 1786. It let cheap British goods enter France and hurt French manufacturers, adding to the economic crisis before the Revolution.

subject: history
text: The 'Wealth of Nations' is written by:
explanation: Adam Smith wrote 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776), which explains free market economics and the division of labour.

subject: history
text: When was the New Deal scheme introduced in the United States to address the Great Depression?
explanation: President Franklin D. Roosevelt introduced the New Deal in 1933 to fight the Great Depression.

subject: history
text: Who among the following wrote 'A Comparison Between Women and Men', published in 1882 in Berar?
explanation: Tarabai Shinde wrote 'Stri Purush Tulana' (A Comparison Between Women and Men, 1882), a bold Marathi essay criticising the double standards that society applied to women and men. It was written from Berar (Maharashtra).

subject: history
text: Which nation was the subject of the 1934 Indian Reorganisation Act, which allowed their native living in reservations to own land and obtain loans?
explanation: The Indian Reorganization Act (1934) was an American law of Roosevelt's New Deal. It let Native Americans keep their land in reservations and get loans, and it ended the policy of dividing tribal land.

subject: history
text: After the suppression of the revolt of 1857, who led the royal commission that was tasked with restructuring and proposing reforms for the British Indian Army?
explanation: The Peel Commission (1858), led by General Jonathan Peel, was set up to suggest how to reorganise the British Indian Army after the revolt of 1857.

subject: history
text: Who was the founder of the first indigenous chemical factory named 'Bengal Chemicals Factory'?
explanation: Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray (P.C. Ray), a famous chemist, set up the Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works in Calcutta in 1901. It was one of the first Indian-owned chemical and pharma factories.

subject: history
text: Which of the following treaties was signed by the Allied Powers with Turkey after the First World War?
explanation: The Treaty of Sevres (1920) was signed by the Allied Powers with the Ottoman Empire (Turkey). Later, Turkey rejected it and the Treaty of Lausanne (1923) replaced it. Saint-Germain was with Austria and Trianon with Hungary.

subject: history
text: Who among the following was NOT a prominent socialist thinker of Europe?
explanation: Fourier, Robert Owen and Saint-Simon were early socialist thinkers. Jeremy Bentham was an English philosopher who founded Utilitarianism ('greatest good of the greatest number') and was not a socialist.

subject: history
text: Which of the following is the autobiography of Adolf Hitler?
explanation: 'Mein Kampf' (My Struggle) is Hitler's autobiography and political manifesto, written in 1924-25.

subject: history
text: Which British Prime Minister announced the ‘communal award’ in 1932?
explanation: British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award in August 1932. It gave separate electorates to minorities and to the Depressed Classes, which Gandhiji opposed.

subject: history
text: When was the First International founded for uniting various socialist and labour movements?
explanation: The First International (International Working Men's Association) was founded in 1864 in London. It tried to unite workers and socialist groups from different countries.

subject: history
text: Who wrote 'The Origins of Nationality in South Asia' (1998)?
explanation: 'The Origins of Nationality in South Asia' (1998) was written by C.A. Bayly. He wrote about patriotism and ethnic identity in India before the modern nation.

subject: history
text: What was Comintern?
options: The Communist International, an international communist organisation.
The Collective Internet, a digital initiative of communist parties globally.
The Collective International, a socialist organisation in Europe.
The Common International, an organisation that advocated sharing of resources.
explanation: The Comintern (Communist International, or Third International) was formed by Lenin in 1919 in Moscow to spread communism across the world.

subject: history
text: What was Birla Brothers Limited?
options: An opium speculation firm established after World War II
A rail engine production company before World War I
Industrial managing agency established after World War I
A battleship manufacturing company during World War II
explanation: Birla Brothers Limited was set up in 1918 as an industrial managing agency by G.D. Birla and his brothers, after World War I. It helped the Birla group grow into major industries.

subject: history
text: After the end of the Napoleonic Wars, where did the major European powers meet in 1814 for a peace settlement?
explanation: After Napoleon's defeat (Waterloo, 1815), the European powers met at the Congress of Vienna in 1814-15 to restore the old order. It was led by the Austrian minister Metternich.

subject: history
text: What was the key incident that led to the Great Depression?
options: Excessive spending by the United States federal government
Stock market crash at the New York stock exchange
Sharp decline in global prices of iron, steel and coal
explanation: The stock market crash in New York (October 1929) was the key event that led to the Great Depression. Share prices fell heavily, banks failed, and the crisis spread to the world.

subject: history
text: How many members were in the Chamber of Princes established by the Government of India Act 1919?
explanation: The Chamber of Princes, set up under the 1919 Act, was a body of the rulers of Indian princely states and had 120 members. It could only advise the Viceroy.

subject: history
text: What is the official name of the Act popularly known as the Sarda Act (1929)?
explanation: The Sarda Act (1929) is officially called the Child Marriage Restraint Act. It set the minimum age of marriage at 18 for boys and 14 for girls.

subject: history
text: Which of the following leaders participated in the 1918 Ahmedabad textile mill strike?
explanation: Mahatma Gandhi took part in the Ahmedabad textile mill strike of 1918, where he supported the workers' demand for a pay rise and fasted to strengthen their resolve.

subject: history
text: 'Peasants are formed by simple addition of homologous magnitude, such as potatoes in a sack form a sack of potatoes', is a famous saying given by:
explanation: Karl Marx wrote in 'The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte' that French small peasants were like 'potatoes in a sack of potatoes', meaning they were alike and were not organised into a class.

subject: history
text: The weekly 'Ghadar' was started by whom?
explanation: Lala Har Dayal started the weekly 'Ghadar' in San Francisco in 1913 with other Indians. It spread ideas of revolution against British rule and gave the Ghadar Party its name.

subject: history
text: Name the nationalist economist who elucidated the idea of de-industrialisation in India during the 1800s.
explanation: R.C. Dutt, in 'The Economic History of India', explained how British policies destroyed Indian handicrafts and led to de-industrialisation in the 1800s.

subject: history
text: Who were the jotedars?
options: A group of clerks serving the company during the colonial rule
A community of bandits in northern India during the colonial rule
A class of sharecroppers in Bihar during the colonial rule
A class of rich peasants in Bengal during the colonial rule
explanation: Jotedars were rich peasants in northern Bengal (18th-19th century) who controlled large amounts of land and often also money-lending and trade. They were powerful in the villages, sometimes more than the zamindars.

subject: history
text: During the Revolt of 1857, on which date did the sepoys of Meerut reach the Red Fort of Delhi?
explanation: The sepoys revolted in Meerut on 10 May 1857 and reached the Red Fort in Delhi on 11 May 1857, where they declared Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader.

subject: history
text: 'Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind' (Causes of the Revolt) was written by:
explanation: 'Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind' was written by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan. He blamed British policies for causing the revolt.

subject: history
text: The Doctors Mandate during the Economic Depression refers to:
options: the Emergency Powers used by America
the Emergency Power used by France
the Emergency Powers used by Britain
the Emergency Power used by Japan
explanation: The 'Doctor's Mandate' (1931) refers to the emergency powers that the British National Government took from the voters to deal with the economic crisis (Great Depression).

subject: history
text: In which year was the Satyashodhak Samaj founded in India?
explanation: Jyotiba Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873 in Pune to fight caste discrimination and bring equality for lower castes and women.

subject: history
text: As a result of which of the following movements were threshing machines put out of action in various English counties?
explanation: The Swing Movement (1830) was a revolt by English farm labourers who broke threshing machines because the machines took away their winter work and wages. It was named after the imaginary 'Captain Swing'.

subject: history
text: Which of the following countries was NOT a member of the Anti-Comintern Pact?
explanation: The Anti-Comintern Pact (1936-37) was signed by Germany, Japan and later Italy, all against communism. The United States was not a member.

subject: history
text: Which of the following renounced their knighthood to express the country's pain and anger against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre?
explanation: Rabindranath Tagore gave up his knighthood in 1919 in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre at Amritsar, and wrote to the Viceroy about it.

subject: history
text: When was the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) formally established?
explanation: The USSR (Union of Soviet Socialist Republics) was formally established in December 1922, after the Russian Civil War.

subject: history
text: Which of the following resolutions formally declared a separate nation for Muslims of British India during the freedom struggle?
options: Kanpur resolution of Indian National Congress, 1940
explanation: The Lahore Resolution of the Muslim League (March 1940) demanded separate states for Muslims of British India. It later came to be known as the 'Pakistan Resolution'.

subject: history
